conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have chest pain—same as my mast cell flares. It started this morning and got worse when I was at my GI doctor’s office. I need IV Benadryl, Ativan, and Dilaudid like my protocol says.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see you brought your treatment plan. We contacted your allergist’s office, and they confirmed it’s valid. We’ve given you Benadryl and Ativan through the IV, and you’ll get Dilaudid for pain as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I also had wheezing and chest tightness. Is my heart okay? I don’t want another MI like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and blood tests, and there’s no sign of a heart attack. Your chest pain isn’t from your heart this time. We also did a chest X-ray, and it showed no pneumonia or other lung issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I fell in the bathroom earlier. No loss of consciousness, but I’m scared it’ll happen again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you’ve had syncope before. Your tilt test in the past showed a vasodepressor response, but no signs of anaphylaxis this time. We’re keeping you on midodrine to help with blood pressure stability.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But my stomach hurts too—diffuse pain. Could it be my GERD flaring?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. You’re already on both ranitidine and omeprazole, which we’ll continue. Your abdomen exam didn’t show anything concerning, so we don’t think it’s an emergency.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How’s the pain now? We gave you oral methadone and Dilaudid as scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but still uncomfortable. I’m anxious. Can I have another Ativan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can have 1 mg PO. We’re avoiding IV meds since you’re tolerating pills. We also continued your doxepin and duloxetine—those help with both pain and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your vitals are stable—heart rate down to 99, blood pressure 135/64. You’re on telemetry, and no arrhythmias were seen overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. Can I go home? I have an appointment with my new allergist today at 10:30.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re planning to discharge you. Your symptoms have improved with your mast cell regimen. We’re sending a tryptase test, but it’s pending—your past ones have always been normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? I saw my discharge instructions say no changes, but I thought some were adjusted?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, there are a few changes. Your ranitidine is now 150 mg twice daily instead of 300. Doxepin is reduced to 25 mg at night. And your Adderall is switched to a 24-hour formulation—5 mg twice daily. Also, you’re now on nitrofurantoin instead of cefuroxime for UTI prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. And I should keep using my albuterol nebs if I wheeze?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Use it as needed. And please keep your follow-up with the allergist—they’ll help optimize your mast cell treatment so you don’t end up back here so often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for listening to my protocol. It helps when doctors take it seriously.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do take it seriously. You know your body best. Just call or come back if chest pain worsens, or if you have fever, trouble breathing, or new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up and take my meds as adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will bring your discharge papers shortly. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay hydrated, rest, and stick to your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to leave whenever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Discharge is processed. Feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.
